query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a thin surface layer of yttrium (Y) onto boride-based components will improve resistance to molten‐aluminum corrosion by promoting the formation of an adherent, aluminum‐rich oxide scale that acts as an effective barrier against aluminum attack.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components (e.g., tungsten or other metal borides) as currently used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment with their native surface state.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface treatment (such as physical vapor deposition followed by a short heat treatment) to incorporate a thin, trace yttrium layer that diffuses into the surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures for durations relevant to industrial plating processes.
generation.structural_mediator: The yttrium that segregates at the boride surface and grain boundaries promotes the nucleation and stabilization of a coherent, aluminum-rich oxide scale with improved adhesion.
generation.mechanism: Yttrium acts as a reactive element that enhances oxide scale adhesion and reduces spallation; by facilitating the formation of a dense, aluminum-rich protective layer, it limits the diffusion of molten aluminum into the substrate and retards corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated boride-based components, the Y-treated surfaces will exhibit a lower weight loss and reduced corrosion damage as measured by thinner or more intact oxide scales after exposure to molten aluminum.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components processed under identical hot-dip conditions without the yttrium surface modification.
generation.boundary: The improved corrosion resistance is expected under standard hot-dip aluminum-plating temperatures (~660 °C) and processing times; effectiveness under significantly higher temperatures or extremely prolonged exposure remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal yttrium concentration and treatment parameters need to be determined, and potential interactions between Y and the boride matrix may affect long-term stability in dynamic plating conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based samples. One set receives the yttrium surface treatment via a controlled deposition and diffusion process, while the control set remains untreated. Both sets will then be subjected to a simulated hot-dip aluminum plating process by immersing them in molten aluminum at ~660 °C for 60 hours. Post exposure, the samples will be cleaned and analyzed using microscopy (SEM/EDS) and weight-loss measurements.
measurements: Weight loss per unit area of each sample
Oxide scale morphology and composition from SEM/EDS analysis
Thickness and adhesion quality of the protective oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in weight loss, improved scale adhesion, or a more protective Al2O3-rich oxide structure compared to the untreated controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. The oxide scale morphologies of the coatings are shown in Figure 10c,g and the EDS analysis is shown in Table 4. It can be concluded that the oxidation corrosion products of the coatings were mainly Al-rich oxides. Additionally, there was also a certain amount of FeCr-rich oxides. Combined with the XRD results in Figure 9, it can be concluded that the corrosion product was mainly Al2O3. By analyzing the morphology and EDS of the corroded areas, it can be concluded that the elemental depletion of the EHEA coating was faster than that of the YHf coating, and trace amounts of sulfur elements were detected in the corroded areas of the EHEA. In conclusion, all coatings exhibited the same corrosion mechanism. The YHf-EHEA coating showed better resistance to the 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts hot corrosion than the EHEA coating at 900 °C.
